source_refs.note: Chapter 14 exercise (PDF 42-44, printed 39-41), solved: 9 MCQs with keys worked out from the chapter (the book prints no key), model answers to 8 short, 6 constructed and 6 comprehensive questions, and 6 numericals worked step by step.

blocks.prompt: 14.1 While determining time period of simple pendulum, we keep the amplitude:
blocks.explanation: The pendulum performs S.H.M only for small angles, where sin θ ≈ θ and a = −(g/ℓ)x. So the amplitude is kept small. With zero amplitude there would be no oscillation to time.

blocks.prompt: 14.2 In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration of a body is zero, when:

options.text: both velocity and displacement are zero
both velocity and displacement are maximum

blocks.explanation: In S.H.M, a = −ω²x. At the mean position x = 0, so a = 0 (while the velocity there is maximum).

blocks.prompt: 14.3 If a tunnel is bored through the centre of Earth and a stone is dropped into it, then:

options.text: stone will stop at the centre of Earth
stone will move out from other side of the tunnel

blocks.explanation: Inside the Earth the gravitational force on the stone is proportional to its distance from the centre and always points to the centre (F ∝ −x). This is a restoring force of the S.H.M type, so the stone oscillates about the centre between the two ends of the tunnel (ignoring air resistance).

blocks.prompt: 14.4 Which of the following variables has zero value at the extreme position in S.H.M?
blocks.explanation: v = ω√(x₀² − x²). At the extreme position x = x₀, so the speed is zero; there the displacement and acceleration are maximum and ω stays constant.

blocks.prompt: 14.5 Which of the following force is responsible for S.H.M?
blocks.explanation: S.H.M is produced by a restoring force that is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position (F = −kx). (An elastic force is one example of a restoring force; the general answer is restoring force.)

blocks.prompt: 14.6 The velocity of a particle moving with S.H.M at the mean position is:
blocks.explanation: At the mean position x = 0, so v = ω√(x₀² − 0) = x₀ω, the maximum velocity.

blocks.prompt: 14.7 A child swinging on a swing in sitting position, stands up, then time period of the swing will:
blocks.explanation: On standing up, the child's centre of mass rises, so the effective length ℓ of the swing (support to centre of mass) decreases. Since T = 2π√(ℓ/g), the time period decreases.

blocks.prompt: 14.8 The total energy of a particle executing S.H.M is proportional to:
blocks.explanation: Total energy T.E = ½kx₀² = ½mω²x₀², so it is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

blocks.prompt: 14.9 The period of simple pendulum increases how many times if its length is doubled?
blocks.explanation: T = 2π√(ℓ/g), so T ∝ √ℓ. With ℓ′ = 2ℓ: T′ = 2π√(2ℓ/g) = √2 T, so the period becomes √2 (about 1.41) times.

blocks.prompt: 14.1 Define simple harmonic motion and write its equation.
blocks.explanation:
Simple harmonic motion is the to and fro motion of a body in which its acceleration is directly proportional to its displacement from the mean position and is always directed towards the mean position.
Equation: a ∝ −x, or a = −ω²x (for a mass-spring system a = −(k/m)x).

blocks.prompt: 14.2 State the basic conditions for frictionless system to execute simple harmonic motion.
blocks.explanation:
1. A restoring force must act that is directly proportional to the displacement and directed towards the mean position (Hooke's law, F = −kx).
2. So the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite to it (a ∝ −x).
3. The body must have inertia (mass), so that it overshoots the mean position and keeps oscillating.

blocks.prompt: 14.3 Differentiate between free and forced oscillations.
blocks.explanation: Free oscillations happen at the body's own natural frequency with no external force; forced oscillations happen under a periodic external (driving) force.

rows: The body oscillates without any external force after being disturbed once
The body oscillates under a periodic external (driving) force
Frequency is the body's own natural frequency
Frequency is the frequency of the driving force
Ideally energy and amplitude stay constant
Amplitude depends on the driving force; it is very large at resonance
Example: a simple pendulum displaced and released
Example: a swing pushed again and again; a factory floor shaken by machines

blocks.prompt: 14.4 Why we cannot construct an ideal simple pendulum? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: An ideal simple pendulum needs a point-mass bob, a weightless and inextensible string, a frictionless rigid support and no air resistance. No real bob is a point, every string has some mass and stretches, and air resistance and friction always act, so an ideal pendulum cannot be made.

blocks.prompt: 14.5 How does sharpness of resonance occur?
blocks.explanation: Sharpness of resonance depends on damping. When damping is small, the amplitude rises steeply to a very large value only near the natural frequency, so the resonance curve is sharp. Heavy damping gives a small amplitude and a flat resonance curve (pith ball vs lead bob experiment).

blocks.prompt: 14.6 What would happen to the time period if the Earth suddenly stop rotating?
blocks.explanation: Because of the Earth's rotation, part of gravity provides the centripetal force, so the effective g is slightly less (except at the poles). If rotation stopped, g would increase slightly everywhere except at the poles, so the time period of a pendulum, T = 2π√(ℓ/g), would decrease slightly (no change at the poles).

blocks.prompt: 14.7 What is restoring force? What provides restoring force for simple harmonic oscillator in the following cases? (i) Simple pendulum (ii) Spring
blocks.explanation:
Restoring force is the force that always acts on a displaced body towards its mean position (F = −kx).
(i) Simple pendulum: the component of the bob's weight along the path, F = −mg sin θ.
(ii) Spring: the elastic force of the stretched or compressed spring, F = −kx.

blocks.prompt: 14.8 What role do shock observers play in oscillations of vehicles in a bumpy road? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation: On a bumpy road the springs of the vehicle start oscillating. Shock absorbers damp these oscillations: they turn the oscillation energy into heat, so the vibrations die out quickly (nearly critical damping) and the passengers get a smooth, comfortable ride.

blocks.prompt: 14.1 Why marching troops are asked to break their steps while crossing a bridge? Explain.
blocks.explanation: Marching in step applies a periodic force on the bridge at the frequency of the footsteps. If this frequency becomes equal to the natural frequency of the bridge, resonance occurs: the bridge vibrates with a very large amplitude and may collapse. Breaking step makes the force irregular, so resonance cannot build up.

blocks.prompt: 14.2 A girl is swinging in the sitting position. Describe, how will the period of swing be changed if she stands up?
blocks.explanation: The swing acts as a simple pendulum with T = 2π√(ℓ/g), where ℓ is the distance from the support to the centre of mass. When she stands up, her centre of mass rises, so ℓ decreases. Hence the time period of the swing decreases (the swing oscillates faster).

blocks.prompt: 14.3 Will a pendulum that keeps correct time at Karachi, be accurate at Murree or at the top of mount Everest? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. T = 2π√(ℓ/g). Karachi is at sea level; Murree and the top of Everest are far higher, where the distance from the Earth's centre is greater and g is smaller. A smaller g gives a longer time period, so the pendulum completes fewer oscillations per day and the clock runs slow (loses time), most of all on Everest. Its length must be shortened to correct it.

blocks.prompt: 14.4 A wire hangs from a dark high tower so that its upper end is not visible. How can we determine the length of a tower?
blocks.explanation:
Tie a small heavy bob to the lower end of the wire so that it forms a simple pendulum. Set it into oscillation with a small amplitude and measure the time period T with a stopwatch (time, say, 20 vibrations and divide by 20). Then
ℓ = gT²/4π²
This length of the pendulum (support to bob) is the height of the tower, adding the small height of the bob above the ground.

blocks.prompt: 14.5 Will the period of a vibrating spring increase, decrease or remain constant by addition of more mass? Explain.
blocks.explanation: It will increase. For a mass-spring system T = 2π√(m/k), so T ∝ √m. Adding mass increases the inertia while the spring constant k stays the same, so the system oscillates more slowly. For example, four times the mass doubles the period.

blocks.prompt: 14.6 Can a simple pendulum vibrate at centre of the the Earth? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. At the centre of the Earth g = 0, so the bob has no weight and there is no restoring force (mg sin θ = 0). From T = 2π√(ℓ/g), T becomes infinite, which means the pendulum does not oscillate at all.

blocks.prompt: 14.1 Show that motion of mass attached to spring executes S.H.M. Also find an expression for its time period and frequency.
blocks.explanation:
Consider a body of mass m attached to a spring of spring constant k on a smooth horizontal surface. Its rest position O is the mean position.
The body is pulled through displacement x. By Hooke's law the applied force is F = kx.
The spring pulls back with an equal and opposite restoring force:
F = −kx ...(1)
When released, the body moves towards O, crosses it due to inertia, compresses the spring and oscillates between the two extreme positions.
By Newton's second law:
F = ma ...(2)
Comparing (1) and (2):
ma = −kx
a = −(k/m)x
As k/m is constant, a = −(constant)x, or a ∝ −x.
The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and always directed towards the mean position, so the motion is S.H.M.
Time period and frequency:
Comparing a = −(k/m)x with a = −ω²x:
ω² = k/m, so ω = √(k/m)
As ω = 2πf:
f = ω/2π = (1/2π)√(k/m)
T = 1/f = 2π√(m/k)
So the period increases with the mass and decreases with a stiffer spring.

blocks.prompt: 14.2 Show that motion of the projection of a particle moving around a circle with constant speed is S.H.M and derive a relation for its instantaneous velocity.
blocks.explanation:
Let particle P move on a circle of radius x₀ with uniform angular velocity ω. Q is its projection (foot of the perpendicular) on the diameter AB; Q moves to and fro along AB about the centre O.
Starting from A at t = 0, the angle swept in time t is θ = ωt.
Displacement: in triangle POQ, OQ/OP = cos θ, so
x = x₀ cos θ = x₀ cos ωt
Acceleration: P has centripetal acceleration aₚ = x₀ω² towards O. The acceleration of Q is its component along the diameter:
a = −aₚ cos θ = −x₀ω²(x/x₀)
a = −ω²x
Since ω is constant, a ∝ −x: the acceleration of Q is proportional to its displacement and directed towards O. Hence the projection executes S.H.M.
Instantaneous velocity: P has speed vₚ = x₀ω along the tangent. The velocity of Q is the component of vₚ parallel to the diameter:
v = vₚ cos(90° − θ) = x₀ω sin θ = x₀ω sin ωt
Using sin θ = √(1 − cos²θ) and cos θ = x/x₀:
v = x₀ω√(1 − x²/x₀²)
v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = √((k/m)(x₀² − x²))
At the mean position (x = 0): v_max = x₀ω; at the extreme position (x = x₀): v = 0.

blocks.prompt: 14.3 What is a simple pendulum? Show that motion of a simple pendulum is S.H.M. Also derive an expression for time period of a simple pendulum, on what factors does it depend?
blocks.explanation:
Simple pendulum: a small heavy bob of mass m suspended from a rigid support by a light, inextensible string of length ℓ.
Proof of S.H.M: displace the bob through a small angle θ and release it. Its weight mg is resolved into mg cos θ (along the string, balanced by the tension) and mg sin θ (along the path, towards the mean position). So the restoring force is
F = −mg sin θ
By Newton's second law F = ma, so
ma = −mg sin θ, a = −g sin θ
For small angles sin θ ≈ θ (in radians):
a = −gθ
With θ = S/ℓ, and the arc S ≈ displacement x for a small angle:
a = −(g/ℓ)x
For a given pendulum at a given place g/ℓ is constant, so a ∝ −x. Hence the motion of a simple pendulum is S.H.M.
Time period: comparing a = −(g/ℓ)x with a = −ω²x:
ω² = g/ℓ, ω = √(g/ℓ)
f = ω/2π = (1/2π)√(g/ℓ)
T = 1/f = 2π√(ℓ/g)
Factors: T is directly proportional to √ℓ and inversely proportional to √g. It does not depend on the mass of the bob, nor on the amplitude (as long as the amplitude is small).

blocks.prompt: 14.4 Derive expressions for K.E. and P.E. of the mass-spring system executing S.H.M. Also prove that its total energy remains same.
blocks.explanation:
Potential energy: to stretch the spring from 0 to x, the force rises from 0 to kx, so the average force is
F_av = (0 + kx)/2 = ½kx
Work done = F_av × x = ½kx × x = ½kx²
This work is stored as elastic potential energy:
P.E. = ½kx²
It is zero at the mean position and maximum, ½kx₀², at the extreme positions.
Kinetic energy: the instantaneous velocity is v = ω√(x₀² − x²) with ω² = k/m, so
v² = (k/m)(x₀² − x²)
K.E. = ½mv² = ½m(k/m)(x₀² − x²)
K.E. = ½k(x₀² − x²)
It is maximum, ½kx₀², at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions.
Total energy:
T.E. = K.E. + P.E. = ½k(x₀² − x²) + ½kx²
T.E. = ½kx₀²
k and x₀ are constant, so the total energy is the same at every displacement: energy keeps changing from K.E. to P.E. and back, but their sum is conserved. With k = mω², T.E. = ½mω²x₀², proportional to the square of the amplitude.
Graph: plotted against x (from −x₀ to +x₀), P.E. is an upward parabola (zero at x = 0), K.E. is an inverted parabola (maximum at x = 0, zero at ±x₀) and T.E. is a horizontal straight line at ½kx₀².

blocks.prompt: 14.5 Explain resonance. Give some of its advantages and disadvantages.
blocks.explanation:
Resonance: when a periodic driving force acts on an oscillating body and its frequency equals the natural frequency of the body (or an integral multiple of it, fₙ = nf₁), the body absorbs energy most effectively and vibrates with a very large amplitude. This is resonance.
Demonstration: pendulums A, B (length ℓ₁) and C, D (length ℓ₂) hang from one horizontal rod. A driving pendulum P of length ℓ₁ is set swinging; A and B (same length, same natural frequency) swing with large amplitude while C and D hardly move. With P of length ℓ₂, C and D resonate instead.
The sharpness of resonance depends on damping: less damping gives a larger and sharper peak.
Advantages (useful resonance):
1. Microwave oven: the microwaves make water molecules in food oscillate at the same frequency; their collisions produce heat that cooks the food.
2. Radio tuning: turning the knob changes the natural frequency of the receiver circuit until it equals the station's frequency; that station's signal is then received strongly.
3. Musical instruments: the sound boards of a piano, violin and guitar resonate with the strings and make the sound loud.
4. Standing-wave demonstrations: Rubens tube, Chladni plate and acoustic levitation.
Disadvantages (resonance to avoid):
1. Bridges: soldiers marching in step may set a bridge into resonant vibration and collapse it; the Tacoma Narrows Bridge (1940) was destroyed by wind-driven resonance.
2. Aeroplane wings: if engine vibration, turbulence or aerodynamic forces match the natural frequency of the wings, resonance may damage them.
3. Buildings: earthquake waves can set buildings into resonance and bring them down (e.g. the 2005 earthquake in Azad Jammu and Kashmir).

blocks.prompt: 14.6 Discuss physical significance of phase in simple harmonic motion, and explain how does it relate to timing and synchronization of oscillation?
blocks.explanation:
Phase: in x = x₀ cos(ωt + φ), the angle (ωt + φ) is the phase of the motion; φ is the phase constant (phase angle), fixed by the displacement and velocity at t = 0.
Physical significance:
1. Phase gives the state of motion of the oscillator at any instant: both its displacement and its direction of motion. Two instants with the same displacement but opposite directions of motion have different phases.
2. For example, with φ = 0 the body is at an extreme position at phase 0, π and 2π, and at the mean position at π/2 and 3π/2.
Relation to timing:
3. The phase increases by 2π in one time period T, so a phase difference Δφ corresponds to a time difference Δt = (Δφ/2π) × T. For example, Δφ = 90° means one oscillator is T/4 ahead of the other.
Relation to synchronization:
4. Two oscillators with phase difference 0° or 360° are in phase: they reach the extreme and mean positions together (synchronized).
5. With phase difference 180° they are out of phase: one is at +x₀ when the other is at −x₀.
6. Graphs of x against t for φ = 0°, 90° and 180° show the same curve shifted in time by 0, T/4 and T/2.
7. In S.H.M the velocity leads the displacement by π/2, and the acceleration is opposite to the displacement (phase difference π).

blocks.prompt: 14.1 A body is executing S.H.M of amplitude 0.05 m and frequency 10 Hz. Find the value of (a) acceleration (b) velocity. (Ans: 197 m s⁻², 3.14 m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: x₀ = 0.05 m, f = 10 Hz
Required: (a) maximum acceleration a_max, (b) maximum velocity v_max
ω = 2πf = 2 × 3.14 × 10 = 62.8 rad s⁻¹
(a) a_max = ω²x₀ (at the extreme position)
a_max = (62.8 rad s⁻¹)² × 0.05 m
a_max = 3948 × 0.05 = 197 m s⁻²
(b) v_max = ωx₀ (at the mean position)
v_max = 62.8 rad s⁻¹ × 0.05 m
v_max = 3.14 m s⁻¹
Answer: a_max = 197 m s⁻², v_max = 3.14 m s⁻¹ (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 14.2 A mass of 0.5 kg is suspended from a spring. The spring is stretched 0.098 m. Find: (i) the period of oscillation of mass when it is given a small displacement. (ii) frequency of oscillation of spring. (Ans: 0.628 s, 1.59 Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 0.5 kg, x = 0.098 m, g = 9.8 m s⁻²
Required: (i) T, (ii) f
At equilibrium the spring force balances the weight: kx = mg
k = mg/x = (0.5 kg × 9.8 m s⁻²)/0.098 m = 50 N m⁻¹
(i) T = 2π√(m/k)
T = 2 × 3.14 × √(0.5 kg / 50 N m⁻¹)
T = 6.28 × √0.01 = 6.28 × 0.1
T = 0.628 s
(ii) f = 1/T = 1/0.628 s
f = 1.59 Hz
Answer: T = 0.628 s, f = 1.59 Hz (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 14.3 A ball of mass 0.5 kg is attached to an elastic spring. The spring is compressed by 10 cm by a force of 45 N. Calculate the energy stored in the spring. What will be the maximum velocity of the ball if the compressing force is suddenly removed? (Ans: 2.25 J, 3 m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 0.5 kg, x = 10 cm = 0.10 m, F = 45 N
Required: P.E. stored, v_max
k = F/x = 45 N / 0.10 m = 450 N m⁻¹
P.E. = ½kx²
P.E. = ½ × 450 N m⁻¹ × (0.10 m)²
P.E. = 225 × 0.01 = 2.25 J
When the force is removed, all this P.E. becomes K.E. at the mean position:
½mv_max² = 2.25 J
v_max² = (2 × 2.25 J)/0.5 kg = 9 m² s⁻²
v_max = 3 m s⁻¹
Answer: 2.25 J, 3 m s⁻¹ (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 14.4 A 80 kg body executes S.H.M with amplitude 30 cm. The restoring force is 60 N, when the displacement is 30 cm. Find: (i) time period (ii) acceleration, Speed, K.E. and P.E. when displacement is 12 cm. (Ans: 1.3 s, 3.0 m s⁻², 1.4 m s⁻¹, 7.6 J, 1.44 J)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 80 kg, x₀ = 30 cm = 0.30 m, F = 60 N at x = 0.30 m, x = 12 cm = 0.12 m
Required: (i) T, (ii) a, v, K.E., P.E. at x = 0.12 m
k = F/x = 60 N / 0.30 m = 200 N m⁻¹
ω = √(k/m) = √(200/80) = √2.5 = 1.58 rad s⁻¹
(i) T = 2π√(m/k) = 2 × 3.14 × √(80 kg / 200 N m⁻¹)
T = 6.28 × √0.4 = 6.28 × 0.632
T = 3.97 s
(ii) Acceleration (magnitude): a = ω²x = (k/m)x = 2.5 s⁻² × 0.12 m
a = 0.30 m s⁻² (towards the mean position)
Speed: v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 1.58 × √((0.30)² − (0.12)²)
v = 1.58 × √(0.09 − 0.0144) = 1.58 × √0.0756 = 1.58 × 0.275
v = 0.43 m s⁻¹
K.E. = ½k(x₀² − x²) = ½ × 200 × 0.0756
K.E. = 7.56 J ≈ 7.6 J
P.E. = ½kx² = ½ × 200 × (0.12)²
P.E. = 1.44 J
Check: K.E. + P.E. = 9.0 J = ½kx₀² = ½ × 200 × 0.09.
Answer: T = 3.97 s; a = 0.30 m s⁻², v = 0.43 m s⁻¹, K.E. = 7.6 J, P.E. = 1.44 J. (The book's K.E. and P.E. agree; its T, a and v do not; see the correction below.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the answers 1.3 s, 3.0 m s⁻² and 1.4 m s⁻¹. These follow from a mass of 8 kg (T = 2π√(8/200) = 1.26 s, a = 25 × 0.12 = 3.0 m s⁻², v = 5 × 0.275 = 1.4 m s⁻¹), not the 80 kg printed in the question. With 80 kg: T = 3.97 s, a = 0.30 m s⁻², v = 0.43 m s⁻¹. K.E. = 7.6 J and P.E. = 1.44 J do not depend on the mass and are right.

blocks.prompt: 14.5 What should be the length of a simple pendulum whose time period is one second? What is its frequency? (Ans: 0.25 m, 1 Hz)
blocks.explanation:
Given: T = 1 s, g = 9.8 m s⁻²
Required: ℓ, f
T = 2π√(ℓ/g)
Squaring: T² = 4π²ℓ/g
ℓ = gT²/4π²
ℓ = (9.8 m s⁻² × (1 s)²)/(4 × (3.14)²)
ℓ = 9.8/39.4 = 0.248 m ≈ 0.25 m
f = 1/T = 1/1 s = 1 Hz
Answer: ℓ ≈ 0.25 m, f = 1 Hz (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 14.6 A block of mass 5 Kg is dropped from a height of 0.8 m onto a spring of spring constant 1960 N m⁻¹. Find the displacement through which the spring will be compressed. (Ans: 0.2 m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 5 kg, h = 0.8 m, k = 1960 N m⁻¹, g = 9.8 m s⁻²
Required: compression x
The loss of gravitational P.E. of the block is stored as elastic P.E. of the spring:
mgh = ½kx²
5 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 0.8 m = ½ × 1960 N m⁻¹ × x²
39.2 J = 980 x²
x² = 39.2/980 = 0.04 m²
x = 0.2 m
Answer: x = 0.2 m (agrees with the book).
Note: this, like the book, takes h as the whole fall. If the block's further fall x while compressing the spring is also counted, mg(h + x) = ½kx² gives 980x² − 49x − 39.2 = 0, so x ≈ 0.23 m.
